notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00550.opp-gr: 1.1 (Greek section 1): εἰς ὑμᾶς βλέψαι is read with its natural sense, the son being unable to face the assembly. §3: ἴ’ νῦν is read as ἔτι νῦν, and the stray 1 before ἂν is taken as a footnote mark. §7: δὶ τι is read as εἴ τι. §8: οὕτ’ ὢ is read as οὕτω. §16: ἑταίραν λελύσθαι is read as 'to have bought a courtesan's freedom'; the middle form is ambiguous.

§25: 'ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ὁ νόμος αὐτός' appears corrupt or elliptical; rendered by supplying '[grants]'. §32: 'νυ γε' read as an ironic affirmative (perhaps ναί γε or νὴ Δία). §37 final sentence is obscure; rendered literally.

38: δεῖτ’ νῶν is a scanning error for δεινῶν; τῶν in 'τῶν ἐπιλανθάνωμαι' read as τὰ δ’ (others). 'The acquitting vote has given up hope' renders ἀπεγνωκέναι... τὴν ἀφιεῖσαν ψῆφον literally; sense: I have despaired of an acquitting vote. 39: φαντίαν is a damaged συκοφαντίαν. 41: ἐλευθερωθέντα read as ἐλευθέρῳ (cf. 'befits a free man'); text uncertain. 48: τοσαύτην ἰσχύν seems to belong to the preceding sentence on nature; text possibly disordered. 53: stray '20' is a page/line number, omitted.

nodes.text: L.
A man indicted his own son for plotting [murder]. The son asks to die untried under the law concerning the untried.

The happier course, citizens, would have been for me not to mount this platform before my time had come, nor ever to speak before you about such matters as I have now come to speak of. But since it is easy to pray for what one wishes, while what necessity demands is what gets done, and necessity cannot be escaped by young or old, I have come to plead with you, a man who cannot even properly look you in the face: on the one hand, because I am no match for the uproar of the assemblies and have no experience of affairs here, I think I could in no way obtain what I am eager for; on the other hand, because you are humane and have been brought up to pity the unfortunate, I hope that you will remove me from the trial and hand me over to my father to be put to death.

2. Now if I were asking you to reconcile my father to me, to make him gentle and to persuade him to lay aside this opinion, which I cannot bear even as a word spoken, perhaps even so I would be seeking nothing foreign to your ways, nor contrary to nature, which wishes children and parents to be close to one another; yet perhaps someone would have been indignant, one of those who do not resemble you, the many, if, having incurred such a charge, I were contriving to give my father neither any account nor any satisfaction. But since what is the end of the trial, if I am convicted, this is what I would wish to undergo in silence, with my father himself doing the work of the vote, I do not know what anyone could look to, or what in all the world he could suspect, that he should not grant the favour.

Now if I saw my father standing here even now and prepared to make speeches to you opposing me, I would have said nothing of what I intend but would have leapt down at once and gone away, knowing well that everything would be said in vain with him contradicting and raging. But since, if nothing else, Fortune has granted us this much, that he is absent from the assembly, occupied with other things, and that those who will oppose [me] are certain others, whom I cannot despise either, but of whom I have no such fear as of him, I have some hope that the pleas of me, so unfortunate, will prevail over their contentiousness.

4. I must, then, speak with tears, citizens, since I now spend my whole life in tears, and neither by day nor by night has any of my household or my friends seen me, since my father's anger, either speaking or keeping silent without tears.

5. And what wonder if I myself am compelled to mourn, when one may see even my companions doing the same as I? For I, the most wicked of men, have all my own comrades from the wrestling-school and the schoolrooms mourning with me and differing in no way in grief from me who am in danger. And I think many of you too will fall into tears on hearing of our misfortunes. So let there be some indulgence for me also, if I cannot tell everything in a continuous way.

6. My father married my mother, as he ought not to have done. I was born and grew up. Nor ought that to have happened. And I escaped many illnesses by which I ought to have died. I was loved by my father, cherished. The boy was everything to him. And no care was lacking: there were tutors, teachers, fees, anxieties, prayers to the gods, a multitude of sacrifices, praises [of me] to other fathers.

If anything troublesome befell him, he took consolation for it from the hopes he had in me; and in the schools I do not know whether I more often called others fortunate or was called blessed by others. And seeing my father caring for the estate and increasing what we had, and enduring every toil so that he might hand the house over to me in good condition, and not being harsh or exacting if I was seen spending something, I rejoiced, and when I went to the temples I began my prayers with my father.

Things going thus for us, shall I tell the rest with frankness? I did not wish to say anything unpleasant about anyone, being still young and having practised, if anyone of my age had, speaking well of everyone, citizens, resident aliens and foreigners alike; but one cannot bear up when wronged.

There are some, citizens, who are vexed at the good fortune of others and think that they themselves are unfortunate amid the prosperity of the many. Of these some groan quietly, others curse and blame Fortune, and others again, bolder than these, cannot bear it unless they overturn households in such a state into the opposite, and they act like enemies, using false words and fabricated charges in place of weapons and siege-engines.

And now they have set husband at war with wife, now uncle with nephew, now brothers with one another, now, as in the present case, father with son; and if they find someone decent and in no way like themselves, they accomplish it easily. For the man who would least plot such things against others himself would most easily be brought down by those who contrive such things.

Would you allow me to say that my father too has become one of those deceived by such men, and that now I am condemned to death because of his goodness? For if what he knew of me over all that time had counted for more with him than what he heard only yesterday, so to speak, none of the present troubles would be driving us. But as it is, my father went out of the house a father to us and came back suddenly an enemy; he glared terribly, struck his thigh, and filled the house with shouting, doing such things then for the first time.

When I asked what was compelling him to do and say these things, he said: "You, whom I have been feeding, not knowing it, as my own murderer." I cried out, citizens, and beat my face with both hands, and called on gods and spirits, and begged him not to commit such impiety.

When he said that he was utterly convinced of this and that no orator could change his mind, I fell at his knees and asked him to exact the ultimate penalty from me. "Here," I said, "is my neck bare for you, here my collarbone, here my chest, all ready to receive the sword. Do not delay, since you have both a hand and a law."

But he shrank from killing his son himself, and spoke of a court and an indictment and another law, the one on plotting. And I thought he would stop there and forget what he had said; but those who, it seems, had thrown in the spark in the first place were fanning his anger. For the reward is no small one: to have our property instead of us. Why say more? The father prosecutes his son for plotting.

Yet I did not run away, although my relatives advised it, on the grounds that time would end his anger and the evildoers would not keep our house shut against us for ever. But I could not bear to be saved shamefully, nor to go with such a charge on me and live among others, nor to give those who had engineered the whole affair the chance to say what they most wished; instead I stay, and I pay the penalty for the suspicion, and I cast the vote against myself. And what need would there be to open a court and measure out the water, when I am drawing the sword upon myself and begging that my father receive me from you and kill me?

16. "But you are asking for something unusual," he says, "compelling a man who wants a trial to slaughter his own son untried." Nor are the charges against me usual ones, citizens, such as drinking more than is moderate, spending time in revels, being devoted to dice, having bought a courtesan her freedom, those things that have enslaved many of the young. Having escaped those things, which is not easy, I alone am charged with things no other young man is. What wonder, then, if new charges have led me on to new arguments?

Apart from this, I am not giving orders to my father today, nor do I stand over him saying: "This you will not do even if you wish; that you will do even if you do not wish; I will not allow you to try me, but I will compel you to kill me." Rather, I have come to you, the humane people, the common father of the young. And my part is supplication; what will come from you is persuasion.

There is a great difference between granting a favour when persuaded and being forced against one's will. The one befits a democracy, the other belongs to tyrants. For not even if I were sending some of my relatives to my father to speak with him about these matters would this be compulsion. For where one could touch his chin and knees and weep and say, "Yield, have pity, kill me yourself, by the gods, by the hearth," what room is there here for the name of compulsion?

If, then, I thought they would suffice, I would not be troubling you, nor would I have taken on a burden greater than befits me by addressing the people; but since they are unequal to the matter, the occasion calls for you, the masters of all things, by whom anyone would pray to be asked for a favour.

20. "So," he says, "will you strike out an indictment that has been lodged?" Not I. How could I? Nor the people either. But he who lodged it [will], if he is persuaded by the people. And he will be persuaded by those from whom he has not seldom received honour. What dishonour, then, is this to my father, if no one will undo what is his against his will, but he himself will undo his own willingly? For they will not dismiss him, call the magistrate and say, "Let the father not be permitted to prosecute his son"; rather, calling the father himself, they will say such things as this to him: "Dearest friend, since you alone of fathers think you are hated by your son, and that the hatred has gone so far as a plot of murder, and you could be persuaded of this, take your satisfaction, we do not beg you off; but take it according to the law, which makes you master of his person. For this, this is what your son begs, freeing you from much trouble, and from these speechwriters."

If the father accepts this and withdraws from the trial, what law has been wronged? What man has been outraged? Which of the citizens has been forced? None. Rather, this one law is confirmed today, the one concerning killings without trial.

Now if I were asking to undergo either no penalty or a small one instead of a greater, as if I came forward and said this: "Citizens, a gang of wicked and malicious men has surrounded our house and is besieging it. Help, before they take it. My father has been won over. He has resolved to take my life himself, a thing which neither happened nor may it happen. For how could I, born from him and knowing this exactly, raised no worse than anyone, and having had a share of education, which can make even the dull better and just and eager for noble deeds, how then could I have thought my father a danger to me, when orphanhood is admitted to be the greatest misfortune? Or is it not sweet to tend an aged father like some divinity, and through care for him to acquire the better hopes? Would I not have feared the laws here? Would I not have feared the terrors in Hades? Make my father gentle to me, then, and master those who are shaking our family apart." If I were asking this, you would rightly be indignant.

And you would rightly be indignant if I said this too: "Let him be angry and take satisfaction, since he wishes to, but by beating, by flogging, by disowning, by driving me from the house, and if this does not suffice, from the city. Only let him allow me to live." These things would cause just anger; at these a man would rightly be indignant.

But as it is, you see that I willingly submit to what is thought the most terrible thing devised by way of punishment, for what could be more terrible than to be no more, and not to enjoy the sun and the other goods which the god has made? To this most terrible thing, then, I willingly go. Let my father cut off my head. If, then, I am ready to suffer even before the trial exactly what I would have suffered, of what, tell me, am I depriving my father?

25. "There is a law," he says, "which grants the father the right to kill his own son untried if he wishes, but does not compel him if he does not wish." Very well. So neither will the law compel him now; but what the law [grants] remains his own. That he should wish it, his son urges through the people. Who, then, could be crueller than those trying to speak against it, who begrudge me a swift end?

26. "But it is madness," he says, "to throw away the uncertainty of a trial and run willingly to certain slaughter." "And why," he says, "if you are doing no wrong, do you fear the trial?" Many things, citizens, many. And first, to have to say, with all of you listening, that my father is lying and making false accusations and inventing things that never happened anywhere.

Someone has indeed said such things before even when contending over trivial matters. But for one whose case concerns death, and on such a charge, and for whom the worse reputation surpasses the penalty, how could he bear these things? For if someone expects me to come in and keep silent, to stand utterly speechless while so many [charges] are pouring down upon me, what do I gain from the trial? And why is a court spent on you to no purpose? But if I must say something and not accept the charge, there is every necessity [to speak] as those in pain and those lamenting do, among which something might escape me that were better left unsaid.

Shall I, then, call my father a false accuser? Shall I say something harsher to him: "Imitate the beasts, father. Even they care for their young"? But first, this is impious and terrible and hateful to gods and divinities, and heavier for me than countless deaths.

Then how great an outcry is it likely there will be, how great an uproar in the court, both from those seated and from those standing around? "The crime is proven, the scheme is exposed. It belongs to one who says such things to have dared that too; words and deeds come from the same soul. If this is in public, what in secret? Will no one strike, will no one kill the murderer of his father?" If, then, silence is a clear admission of the charge and speech would have the same effect, what benefit is the court to the defendant?

But let us suppose that you wish me to have complete freedom for every word, and that no one will gag or hinder me or take offence at anything said; yet, inexperienced in courts as I am, citizens, and young, and of the age you see, and alone, how shall I bear up against my father's old age, his title, his experience of affairs, the crowd of orators, and those who profit from my death?

Who will stand by me, who will defend me, who will help, if none of the older men will wish to and none of the young will be able to? The former, out of respect for their own age, will share my father's anger; the latter would not even dare to peep into the court. How could they, who grow dizzy if they meet several of you in the narrow streets?

But will someone stand by me in hope of money? From where? Or someone who has been well treated and is repaying a favour? What favour? For I love all of you, citizens, and your children, as the gods know, but to have conferred great benefits on any men is not for us young ones. Slaves, by Zeus, will be on our side? Yes indeed, my father's slaves, who know the fetters and the mill. What then? To whom shall I look? Whom shall I supplicate? Whom shall I question? To whom shall I reply? How shall I escape such great breakers?

33. "But who that spoke justly has been defeated?" In the courts before now one who owed a penalty has not paid it, and another who did not owe one has been punished. And just as torrents often carry away the works built to protect the fields, so the share of justice is swept away by a faction of flatterers and by more august names, such as my father's is. For even if I came in with all the other advantages, none of which I now have, his raised eyebrows would be enough for my father, and his nods, and a faint voice, and a downcast face, and the cry, "O gods, why did I marry?"

So I shall perish in nothing else than the form of a trial, and, seeming to share equal terms, I shall fall into an unequal contest. For one to whom every plea is useless for safety and whose conviction is certainly foreseen, how would I not be foolish if I did not forestall the jurors?

"Because," he says, "they will swear an oath, and not even if they very much wished would they favour either side. For fear will prevent them." I would not accuse those who will vote of neglecting their oaths, but I know that many jurors have often been deceived, and this though they had taken no little care not to be misled.

How does this happen? The juror comes to learn from the litigants about what he will vote on. And these sometimes inform him adequately, and sometimes not. Often some of them are clever at twisting the truth in speech, while others cannot set out adequately the facts they have. Here, then, justice is defeated and at the same time the oath is not transgressed. For one who misses what is right unwillingly is free of blame.

And the lawgiver is a witness to this, having made mention of deception and invoking a curse on deceivers on behalf of those misled. If he had known that justice would prevail everywhere, there would not be in the laws the name either of deceivers or of the deceived. But knowing that courts cannot be wholly free of deception, and wishing to prevent it, he found nothing else for this purpose and thought there need be only the curse. But slight, it seems, is the account this takes of equality and justice.

If, then, they do what clever speakers and sophists do, while I stand thunderstruck and dizzy, and fail to find some things and forget others, and appear to differ little from statues, is this now an accusation against the jurors? What then? If they ask, "What do you say to this, boy? How do you claim you are being falsely accused?" and my father's face turns my tongue aside, would the defendant's sense of shame be a fault in the juror? What sort of fault? So let no one think I am accusing those who will judge, when I say that the acquitting vote has given up hope. For it is not because I suspect them, but because I blame myself, that I can make this guess.

But if I must concede this too, and grant that what will never happen will happen admittedly, [namely] that they will think the charges false and that there has never been a false accusation more evident than this, and will rebuke the accuser and his people and pity my isolation, know well that I fear this also. And now for me, wretch that I am, to be convicted is the greatest misfortune, and to be acquitted is no small one, and even to be put on trial on such absurd grounds is unbearable.

Take a general, loyal to those who trusted him and harsh to the enemy, who was tried on the ground that he was advancing their interests, and on trial was acquitted. Not being convicted does not console him; having been tried pains him, and such a man would not even wish to live. A doctor likewise, who has used every device for the sick all his time, but has undergone a trial on the charge of willingly adding to their diseases: would he count it a gain, even if he escapes death?

For if someone incurs the charge from which he stands farthest, the thing is unbearable even to one who prevails. For somehow the shame remains, even if the death [penalty] is lifted, and the man struck by it must either bow to the ground like someone disenfranchised, or, speaking as befits a freed man, endure the reproaches arising from the indictment.

So for me myself it is not tolerable to live under such suspicions. For I know what I shall hear even if I survive: "The father's murderer, the one who brought such great evil upon the house, is he to go to temples? Is he to set foot in the marketplace? Is he to take part in assemblies?"

But indeed I have forgotten myself, expecting acquittal and the sort of words that await me as victor. For where is my victory to come from? What will make a son more powerful than his father in a court? What fortune?

44. "But the father," he says, "will be ill spoken of for having killed [him] untried." For one who wishes to revile [him] will say that a son who had done no wrong is dead. But if he goes to trial, my good man, will he escape this? Will there not then too be people saying: "A young man was snatched away by false accusation. The father buried his son under slanders. He swamped with the voices of trained orators one who did not even know well where on earth he stood"? Do you think, citizens, that a son defeated by his father in court will ever be thought to have been justly defeated? Father is not so small a name.

Since, then, the same reputation will surround him either way, I spare my father the many things: the need for court officials, for jurors, for speeches from those who do anything to get something. They hang about him every day, and groan indeed, and call me accursed and impious and all such things. And I know that for each of these words each of these men goes away carrying something. From these I free my own father, moving him on to the deed, which cuts all these many things short. For what could be quicker than to take up a sword and strike one who does not fight back?

46. "But this is hard for a father," he says, "and perhaps not even possible. For there is no example by which he might be encouraged. For nowhere does this law appear to have been put into action." Add, if you like, also these things that are repeated everywhere and by everyone: that this law, which says that killings of sons may be without trial, wants sons to fear this power and to behave modestly because of it, but grants no one leave to kill, nor to fill the city with a pollution that no one could wash away. I have heard this often; but nevertheless let my father alone kill, since he alone is the father of a son so eager to die.

47. "But nature," he says, "will stand in the way." What nature? The one that I, as he himself says, have shown to be rotten? Long ago these were the words: to adorn nature and call her a goddess and greatest of the gods, she who reaches even through the creeping things themselves, displaying her own strength, who persuades fathers to face danger before their sons, and these before their fathers. Battle lines and fights and slaughter and the passion for dying in arms, it is she that causes them. She teaches some to buy freedom for their offspring with their lives, and others [to buy it] for those from whom they themselves were born.

These laws time kept unbroken until my audacity; but I myself, as he himself shouts, exposed so great a strength and destroyed and trampled on the ordinance. And when indeed I mentioned nature to him at home, he scorned it. So let him admit it, and not think it now nothing, now something great.

Let him put away the thought of his son and say to himself: "You will not kill a son." No, but an enemy, a foe, an adversary. For if he is not persuaded of this, why does he push for the trial? Why does he deprive the house of a son who has done no wrong? But if no one could remove this from his mind, let him judge his son by his character, not by his seed.

50. Call my father, then, and announce the favour: let him take me over from you like some captive. Whether he wishes to kill me here before the eyes of the whole people, let him kill; or in the council chamber with the council in session, let him slay; or in front of the court, let him strike; or in the middle of the marketplace, let him smite. Perhaps the men's hall of the house would suit the deed, where, dining with my father, I did not respect even the table itself. Let him call the whole kindred, and having stationed men and women around my body, at sunrise, after speaking much against me to himself, so let him cut me down.

51. But he could do none of these things. Very well. But this at least is easiest: to hand me over for slaughter to the first who spoke to him this [charge] about me. I shall bear them too as they bring the sword upon me. And if they too should shrink from the killing, which I would wonder at, he will have one of the household slaves in his place. He will not be wholly at a loss for a slayer. When, then, he has thus gratified his anger, let him make peace with the corpse and put an end to his wrath and grant some favour to the dead. Many have wept over those, lying dead, with whom they warred while they lived.

Do you think I shall mention a tomb and a mound or any such thing that could console a soul departing thus? Not at all. Therefore I ask the opposite. Let no tomb of mine be visible, nor let anyone be able to stand by and say, "So-and-so, son of so-and-so, lies here"; but let it be unknown where I am hidden, and let a farmer plough and sow above. Or rather, let my father cast me out unburied. Better still, perhaps, if he should sink me in the sea.

53. To those of my own age I shall say this much and stop: O partners in education and in the finest pursuits, that you are good and just and loving to your fathers I know well; yet you must fear that this evil, beginning somehow from me, may cast many of those now praised into a similar reputation. Guard everything, then, and watch closely, and see that nothing unnoticed overturns the happiness you now have. This is of benefit not more to you than to the whole city.

54. As for my father, if he greatly desires a court and a trial, let him kill me now, and after that, dead himself in Hades, let him prosecute me, dead, before the judges there, where the one and only advantage is the weight of justice.
